name: Chamorro people
info: The Chamorro, or CHamoru, are the Indigenous people of the Mariana Islands in Micronesia, seafarers who arrived about 1,500 BC, built on latte stones, and today live on Guam, the Northern Marianas and across the United States.

facts.homeland: The Mariana Islands, divided between the United States territory of Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, among them Guåhan (Guam), Luta (Rota) and Saipan; large communities also live in Hawaii, California, Washington, Texas and other US states
facts.period: Arrival in the Marianas c. 1,500 BC; the Unai and Latte periods; Spanish rule 1521–1898; United States rule of Guam from 1898, with German and Japanese rule in the Northern Marianas; Japanese occupation of Guam 1941–1944; a living people today
facts.known: the latte stone, now a national symbol; seafaring and outrigger canoes; weaving and pottery; the matrilineal clan; the creation story of Puntan and Fu’una; the value of inafa’maolek, “doing good for each other”; red rice and kelaguen
facts.sources: Spanish colonial and missionary records (Charles Le Gobien, Pierre Coomans), the account of Christoph Carl Fernberger of 1623, archaeology, DNA studies of ancient remains, Chamorro oral tradition, and United States census figures

t: The Chamorro language belongs to the Malayo-Polynesian subgroup of the Austronesian family and took many Spanish loanwords in more than 300 years of Spanish rule.
During the Japanese occupation of Guam from 1941 to 1944, Chamorros were subjected to forced labour, imprisonment, torture and execution.
Chamorro institutions on Guam advocate the spelling CHamoru, which the language commission announced as the preferred standard in 2018.
dyk: In the Chamorro creation story the dying Puntan had his sister Fu’una make the world from his body: his eyes became the Sun and Moon and his eyebrows the rainbows.

sections.origins:
The Chamorros are commonly believed to have arrived in the Mariana Islands from the Philippines around 1,500 BC. They are most closely related to other Austronesian-speaking peoples of the Philippines, eastern Indonesia, Taiwan and the Caroline Islands to the south. Recent DNA testing of the remains of ancient Chamorros, however, showed that the lineage of both the Unai and the Latte periods began in eastern Indonesia, most likely Sulawesi, with no direct prehistoric connection to the Philippines.

The Chamorro language is part of the Malayo-Polynesian subgroup of the Austronesian family. The name has a colonial history. In precolonial society Chamori was the name of the ruling, highest caste; under Spanish rule the caste system died out and all the Indigenous people of the islands came to be called by the Spanish exonym Chamorro. CHamoru is the endonym, written in the Indigenous orthography, with ch treated as a single letter. Guam Public Law 33-236 of 2017 reflects that spelling, and in 2018 the Commission on the CHamoru Language announced it as the preferred standard.
sections.society:
Chamorro society was built on what the sociologist Lawrence J. Cunningham called the matrilineal avuncuclan, in which a mother’s brothers play a greater paternal role than a child’s father. Life still centres on the matriarchal clan descended from a common female ancestor, and large extended families remain central in the Marianas.

Society was divided into two main castes, a division that lasted well over a century after the Spanish arrived. The higher Chamori were subdivided into the upper-middle Achoti and the ruling Matua; Achoti could rise to Matua and Matua fall to Achoti, but the Manachang were born and died as such, and the two castes could not intermingle. All three classes did physical labour, with different duties. Spanish colonial records show farmers planting by the phases of the moon, and farmers on Guam still plant sweet potato and yams at full moon during low tide. Archaeology shows that rice was grown in the Marianas from prehistory. The early Chamorros were expert seafarers, and outrigger canoes served in war, fishing and sailing.
sections.beliefs:
In Chamorro legend the world was made by the twin brother and sister Puntan and Fu’una. As he lay dying, Puntan told his sister to make his body into the universe: his eyes became the Sun and Moon, his eyebrows rainbows. Fu’una then came down on Guåhan and turned herself into a rock, which split, and from it all human beings came. Some place the rock at a church in Agat, others at the Laso de Fua in Fouha Bay in Umatac. Villages on Guam are named after parts of the body: Barrigada means flank, Tiyan stomach, Mongmong a heartbeat.

Ancient Chamorros venerated their ancestors but did not worship deities in a formal religion. The taotaomo’na, “people of early times”, are the spirits of ancient Chamorros, believed far stronger than people and able to bring sickness and death on those who offend them. Under Spain the missionaries worked to convert the people, and those caught practising “sorcery” were publicly punished. Most Chamorros today are Roman Catholic; some still ask the ancestral spirits’ permission before entering parts of the jungle, and the healers called suruhånu are respected for their knowledge of herbs and spirits.
sections.arts:
The early Chamorros were skilled craftspeople, known for intricate weaving and detailed pottery. Their best-known work is the latte stone, a megalithic rock pillar topped with a hemispherical capstone, which served as the foundation for buildings and has since become a national symbol. Missionaries recorded that women blackened their teeth, which they thought beautiful, a custom also widespread in ancient maritime Southeast Asia and Japan. Both sexes wore hats woven from leaves against the sun.

CHamoru dance carries chant and storytelling with it. Dance costumes were traditionally woven and crafted: women wore mestiza dresses and men a sadí of cotton or linen. An important movement is shaped by the canoe, performed with the hands or with wooden sticks. Chamorro cuisine has its own dishes and borrowings: red rice coloured with achoti is a staple of fiestas, nobenas and graduations; kelaguen is meat cooked by citric acid rather than heat; tinaktak is meat in coconut milk; fina’denne’ goes with most meals; and empanadas and pancit came from Spain and the Philippines.
sections.exchange:
On 6 March 1521 Ferdinand Magellan’s men reached the islands after crossing the Pacific. Spain annexed and colonised the Marianas and ruled them until 1898, converting the people to Catholicism and giving them Spanish surnames from the Catálogo Alfabético de Apellidos; in 1672 a Chamorro man angered by the baptism of his child killed the priest Diego Luis de San Vitores and the catechist Pedro Calungsod. In the Spanish era Chamorros began to interact closely with Spaniards and Filipinos.

The United States captured Guam in 1898, while the Northern Marianas came under German and then Japanese rule. Japanese forces invaded Guam on 8 December 1941, and during the occupation of two and a half years Chamorros were subjected to forced labour, incarceration, torture and execution. Chamorros from the Northern Marianas were brought in to help the Japanese administration, which opened a rift that later led Guam’s Chamorros to reject reunification. American forces recaptured the island on 21 July 1944. The Guam Organic Act of 1950 gave the people US citizenship, but Guam remains one of the 17 non-self-governing territories listed by the United Nations.
sections.legacy:
According to the 2020 census, about 63,035 people with Chamorro ancestry live on Guam and 17,163 in the Northern Marianas, and roughly 168,226 Chamorros live in the United States as a whole. Migration began in the first decade of the 20th century and grew after the Second World War, often through military service; enlistment rates in the Marianas are higher than anywhere else in the United States. San Diego County has the largest Chamorro population on the mainland.

Chamorro culture has taken in Spanish, Mexican, American, Japanese and Filipino influences, but holds to inafa’maolek, “doing good for each other”, and respect for family, community and the elderly. The language is spoken in fewer homes than before, yet all public schools on Guam and in the Northern Marianas must now teach it. On Guam a Chamorro rights movement seeks the return of ancestral lands and self-determination. The brown tree snake brought in during the Second World War has decimated the islands’ birds and threatens the fruit bat, once used in kå’du fanihi soup.

summary: The Chamorro are the Indigenous people of the Mariana Islands, Austronesian seafarers who arrived about 1,500 BC and built on latte stones. Ruled in turn by Spain, Germany, Japan and the United States, and brutally occupied by Japan in 1941–1944, they keep their language, matrilineal clans and values today, on Guam, in the Northern Marianas and across the United States.

Event 1672 is given as April 1672 in the article; the event year only is used.
